extracted.intended_audience: applicants and practitioners preparing European patent applications (inventors, patent attorneys, examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing inventive step for European patent applications under Article 56 EPC, explaining the problem‑solution approach, role of indicia (e.g. long‑felt need), admissible combination of prior art, and the skilled person standard at the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 56 EPC — non‑obviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention shall be considered as involving an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quote from Art.56 EPC. Also: 'If the state of the art also includes documents within the meaning of Article 54, paragraph 3, these documents shall not be considered in deciding whether there has been an inventive step.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled person (objective legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment is not the subjective achievement of the inventor but what problems an average skilled person in the art had to overcome; the individual history of the invention is irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'average skilled person' is a legal fiction: 'The same invention that may have seemed a piece of cake for a top specialist ... may have appeared to a beginner ... And yet, the achievement of both inventors is measured by the same standard.' Evaluation must be from that objective viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indications of inventive step (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstantial indicia (e.g. long‑felt need, failure of others) may indicate inventive step but are not a substitute for technical assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'an indication is for example that although a need for an invention existed for a long time, no disclosure could be found that this problem was solved before.' Caveat: absence of prior solution may have other explanations (e.g. solution was too expensive), and such indicia do not automatically establish inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑solution approach (EPO standard method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity is achieved by identifying the objectively ruling state of the art, determining the technical problem the invention addresses, and assessing whether the disclosed solution would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps emphasized: (1) start from the objectively ruling state of the art; (2) determine the technical problem from an objective point of view; (3) consider obviousness of the disclosed solution as seen by the skilled person 'having those capabilities which can be objectively expected of him.' The page stresses that indications are no substitute for this technically skilled assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal viewpoint — priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step must be assessed from the point of view of the skilled person at the time of priority relevant for the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, 'all previously published embodiments must be taken into consideration which offered a suggestion to the skilled practitioner for solving the problem addressed, even where those embodiments were not particularly emphasised (T 0024/81).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on inadmissible 'mosaic' combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inadmissible to mosaically combine unrelated or conflicting documents to deny inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, it is permissible to consider various publications jointly to prove a prejudice or a general trend in the art pointing away from the invention (reference to T 0002/81). In other words, arbitrary piecing‑together of unrelated disclosures to make the invention obvious is not allowed, but consistent joint consideration to show a technical trend or expectation is admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative explanations for indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on secondary indicia (e.g. long‑felt need, commercial success), examiners/applicants must weigh alternative reasons why the invention was not made earlier (e.g. cost, competitiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page warns: 'The reason no‑one made the invention before could also lay in the fact that the solution was regarded as too expensive, and therefore not competitive with the prior art solution. ... the invention may have been a mere choice between equally suitable solutions.' Thus indicia require contextual analysis.
